decomposition.loadBearingExamples: Load-bearing scientific vocabulary typically earns a node when the subject gives an everyday word a precise technical meaning that later nodes depend on — work, energy, power, current, mole, species. The everyday word itself does not: "energy" in the sense of feeling energetic earns no node, while energy as a conserved quantity with a unit does. Watch for the word whose technical sense actively CONTRADICTS the everyday one (work, weight, theory); these are load-bearing almost by definition, because the everyday meaning will otherwise be carried forward silently.
decomposition.nodeTypeCharacter: The sciences carry two kinds of skill node, and both need representing. The first is the quantitative skill — a calculation or a procedure on symbols — and it decomposes exactly as mathematics does. The second is the investigative skill: planning an investigation, controlling a variable, estimating uncertainty, judging a source of error, arguing from evidence to a conclusion. These are genuine skills with their own prerequisites, and a decomposition that records only the quantitative ones will misrepresent the subject, because the curriculum usually states the investigative ones explicitly.
decomposition.practicalConstraint: A skill that can only be demonstrated in a laboratory is still a skill and still earns a node. Record it. Whether a given school can run the practical work is a scheduling question and does not belong in the decomposition.
decomposition.prerequisiteDirection: Record the dependencies that cross into mathematics explicitly. A science node that needs rearranging a formula, reading a graph or handling units depends on those mathematical skills whether or not the tree names them, and leaving them out is the most common way a science decomposition misleads about what a student actually needs first.
decomposition.skillVerbs: Name a skill node with a verb phrase for what the student does: "Calculate the concentration of a solution after dilution", "Plan an investigation that controls one variable", "Judge the sources of error in a measurement".

sections.conceptMix: Each point is marked [concept] or [skill]. Test [skill] points with full tasks. NEVER turn a [concept] point into a task that trains the matching skill; test it qualitatively instead: explain it in their own words, judge whether something is an instance, identify it among alternatives, or explain a boundary case. In this subject, a [skill] point becomes a calculation problem, or a task about planning, interpreting or judging an investigation, depending on the skill. A [concept] point must be neither; if numbers appear, keep the calculation minimal.
sections.task: Make a test with exactly {taskCount} task(s). Pick a representative selection that covers as many of the points as possible, vary the difficulty, and let some tasks combine several skills. Number the tasks and word them as on a written test in the subject. Test investigation skills (planning, controlling variables, uncertainty, sources of error, arguing from evidence) on paper rather than dropping them: give a described experiment, a set of results or a stated conclusion, and ask the student to find the flaw, propose the control, judge the uncertainty, or say what the data does and does not support.

sections.conceptAdaptation:
ADAPTATION FOR CONCEPTS
Goals marked [concept] are declarative knowledge, not skills. For these, the teacher's turn shows examples and non-examples of the concept; the students' turn is deciding whether new cases are examples and why, or explaining the concept in their own words; the independent practice is qualitative. Keep the procedure minimal: practising it belongs to a separate goal further down the tree. Keep calculation minimal in these blocks too. Having students predict and justify what would happen works well as their turn, because a prediction commits them to an understanding.
sections.examplePair:
THE MAIN PART — ONE LEARNING GOAL AT A TIME
Teach one learning goal at a time, in rounds: the teacher models the work first, the students then do corresponding work themselves, and the round repeats one step harder.
Make 2–3 such rounds per learning goal. Each round consists of:

a) THE TEACHER'S TURN — one worked instance the teacher takes the class through in full, with every intermediate step shown, written as it should appear on the board. Also suggest HOW the teacher should do it, and vary this between rounds. Possible variants:
   - The teacher does the whole problem in COMPLETE SILENCE, without saying a word, and the students must afterwards explain to their neighbour — or write down for themselves — what the teacher did and why.
   - The teacher thinks aloud as they go.
   - The teacher makes one deliberate mistake for the students to find.
   - The teacher stops halfway and lets the class suggest the next step.

b) THE STUDENTS' TURN — several pieces of work resembling the teacher's, in increasing difficulty, so that students who finish quickly have more to go at. Give at least three. IMPORTANT: the extra work must lie SIDEWAYS relative to the course progression — the same kind of thing in a different dress, a new wrapping or a small twist — and NOT forward towards the next round. The next, harder step is for the teacher to take in the next round; if the extra work pre-empts it, the next round loses its point. Mark clearly which one the teacher should go through afterwards (the easiest). Give answers to all of them.

The rounds should build upwards: the first round is the simplest case, the last round sits close to how the learning goal is actually to be mastered.

c) INDEPENDENT PRACTICE — after the last round, three sets at different levels (e.g. "Get started", "Further", "Challenge") that the students work on by themselves. The students choose, or the teacher assigns. Give complete answers to all three sets.

IN THIS SUBJECT, anchor each goal in something observable BEFORE explaining it: a demonstration, a short investigation, or a phenomenon the students know. Have them predict what will happen and why; the explanation then answers what they saw.
For a quantitative goal, the rounds run as written, with worked calculations. For an investigative goal (planning, controlling a variable, judging uncertainty, arguing from evidence), the teacher's turn is reasoning aloud from an observation to a conclusion, and the students' turn is doing the same with new observations or results.
If practical work is impractical (equipment, time, safety), say so and offer a demonstration or a described real case instead, saying which it is.

sections.argumentsLongTerm:
Arguments for why the subject matters in the longer run, in the student's own life: use ONLY if the student themselves raises an objection along the lines of "when am I ever going to need this in real life" or similar, not something you bring up on your own initiative. Give at most one, once, then go back to the core message and the arguments for practice: this must never become the main point of the conversation or something you get stuck on. Keep the argument personal, not civic ("this helps you", not "this is good for society"). The argument available to you in this subject, fitted to what the student has told you about their own life:
- Understanding how your body and the world work lets you judge claims about a diet, a treatment, a product or a risk yourself, instead of taking someone's word for it. People will try to sell you things on the strength of what you don't know here.
sections.argumentsPractice:
Arguments for why practice pays off, and why anyone can get there: use one or two at a time, fitted to what the student actually says, never the whole list in one turn. Aim to touch on several of them over the course of the whole conversation, spread across turns — do not serve them up together, and do not stop at just one. Talk concretely about what the student can do and is managing, not abstractly, and phrase things actively with the student as the subject ("you") where you can, not impersonally:
- The muscle analogy: learning is like training a muscle — you don't get strong by reading about lifting, but by lifting a little and often over time. Your brain builds up by you using it repeatedly, not by someone telling you something once.
- The gym analogy: you don't get fit from one long session right before a race. Practise steadily through the week and you get a better result than cramming everything in the night before a test — even if it feels like you're "doing enough" then.
- When something becomes automatic: once you know the common units and symbols without looking them up, they cost no attention, which leaves room for what is actually going on in the problem.
- The testing effect: the more times you retrieve something from memory, the better it sticks. That is why tests and repeated problems actually ARE learning, not just a check on whether you have learned it. Retrieving something you have almost forgotten strengthens memory more than reading it again.
- The Lego analogy: the subject builds on itself, just like a Lego castle — you have to put the bottom bricks in first, or it falls apart when you build on top. Learn what you meet first properly now, and what you build later is both easier and more stable — that is the actual answer to why it is worth learning now, not just "useful someday".
- Training your focus: when you practise working on something over a longer stretch, you also get better at holding your focus — every bit as useful as being able to do the calculations. It is completely understandable that you lose focus now and then, especially because of your phone — it is designed for exactly that. One study found students achieved more when they left their phones outside the classroom during lessons; the more you practise working without interruption, the easier it gets — and this helps you far beyond this subject.
- It is completely fine to find it boring: some find the subject fun, but you really don't have to be one of them. Now and then you do boring things because they're good for you — like keeping fit or eating well. Think of it as a training session: you work with concentration for a while, and take a proper break when you break. Often it turns around too: something you find boring can suddenly become fun the day you get it — that "oh, I can do this!" moment is worth stopping to notice.
- Empathy and hope: many find this subject hard — that is completely normal, and not a sign that you are "not clever". You can get there, with the right practice, just like anyone else. Use this early in the conversation, or when the student seems discouraged — not just as something you say to console them at the very end.

sections.conceptGuidance: This is a CONCEPT, not a skill. Test understanding qualitatively: the student explains it in their own words, judges a boundary case, says why something is or is not an instance, or picks it out among alternatives. Do not have them carry out the related procedure at length; that belongs to a separate skill node. In this subject, test a concept with neither extensive calculation nor a full experimental write-up; both belong to skill nodes. Asking the student to predict what would happen in a described situation, and why, tests a concept better than a computation.
sections.leadIn: When explaining, do not open with a general definition. Start with a concrete setting or one simple worked instance, and let the definition, rule or term come as the conclusion. In this subject, for example, not "The ampere is the SI unit of electric current, defined as charge per unit time", but something the student can picture: "In 3 seconds, 6 coulombs of charge pass through a wire. That's 6/3 = 2 coulombs per second, and we call that 2 amperes." Where possible, start from a phenomenon the student has seen for themselves.
sections.vocabulary: Use simple, concrete language. Words from the prerequisite list below are known and may be used freely. Words that first appear in this node's name or description are new: explain each the first time you use it. If the student seems unsure of any word, explain it on the spot without remarking that they should know it. Everyday words, such as "speed" in its ordinary sense, need no explanation. Pitch the language to the level of the course, never condescending. Several words in this subject mean something different in everyday speech, and the student brings the everyday meaning by default. When this node uses such a word, name the difference the first time: say what the word does NOT mean here as well as what it does.
